chunks: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Ashʿarī narrated from al-Sindī ibn Muḥammad, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, from Abū Maryam, who mentioned it from his father:

Umāmah bint Abī al-ʿĀṣ—whose mother was Zaynab bint Rasūl Allah صلى الله عليه وآله—was married to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib عليه السلام after Fāṭimah عليها السلام. After ʿAlī عليه السلام, al-Mughīrah ibn al-Nawfal succeeded him as her husband.

He mentioned that she became severely ill until her tongue was restrained, so al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, the two sons of ʿAlī عليهما السلام, came to her while she was unable to speak. They began speaking to her, while al-Mughīrah disliked that.

"Did you free so-and-so and his family?" She began indicating with her head, yes. "And such-and-such?" She again began indicating with her head that yes, while not speaking clearly, so that was deemed valid for her.

key_terms.أَعْتَقْتِ: You emancipated; a declaration of freeing a slave
key_terms.اعْتُقِلَ لِسَانُهَا: her tongue became restrained; she lost the ability to speak
key_terms.فَأَجَازَ ذَلِكَ لَهَا: that was accepted as valid for her
key_terms.لَا تُفْصِحُ بِالْكَلَامِ: she could not articulate speech clearly

ai.seo_question: Are a dying person's gestures legally valid when they are unable to speak?
ai.summary: This hadith relates that Umāmah bint Abī al-ʿĀṣ, when rendered unable to speak by severe illness, communicated her intentions by nodding her head. The narration establishes the legal validity of clear gestures in place of speech when a person cannot speak, especially in matters such as manumission and bequest-related declarations.
